Solely for discussion's sake I will try to provide the counter argument. I am only trying to have a civil conversation; this is not a personal attack against anyone that does not support copyrights.

Say, for instance, that you are a successful author that published 5 novels during your career. You, your wife and child live from the royalties that you perceive from the books' sales. Due to an unfortunate accident or illness, you die. Since copyrights extinguish after the death of the author, the publishing house immediately ceases to pay any royalties to your heirs upon death.

While a little extreme, I hope that that scenario provides a fairly reasonable argument in favor of extending copyright protection after the death of the author.

Copyrights are property, except immaterial. When you die, all property passes on to your heirs. So is the case for copyrights, except with a limitation as to time. Ending this property abruptly is undesirable, but instead you want a reasonable time frame for the copyright asset to slowly loss it's value. Otherwise it'd be a huge risk for someone that wants to invest in living from copyrights!

In my view, at the very least there is a public interest in making sure that the value copyrights are not strictly tied to the author. There are other reasons, of course, such as encouragement of enterprises focused on the production of assets that incorporate copyrights. However, this is where things become more controversial.

There has been a trend on extending the longevity and coerciveness of copyrights. I do not support this. Especially, in the context of predatory companies like Disney, multi-national trade treaties, etc. But, I do not think that their outright abolishment of copyrights after the death of the author is reasonable.

Say instead, for instance, that I am a successful programmer. I, my wife and child live from my paycheck that I receive for my expertise. Due to an unfortunate accident or illness, I die. Since I can no longer work after my death, the company immediately ceases to pay any paychecks to my heirs upon death.

Suddenly it doesn't sound so weird, does it?

If you want to take care of your heirs in the case of your untimely death - buy life insurance like everyone else. Why should authors be any different? Why should they be able to provide for their families from beyond the grave? They should make any necessary preparations just like everyone else.

Personally, I don't even think copyright should survive until the author's death. I think it should be X years after the work is first publicly available (no matter when the author dies). 17-20 years seems like a good length of time to me.

I think we're all on the same page. We may disagree on some of the finer details but the general idea here is that death+70 years is insanity and that some kind of static limit, regardless of death, is a good idea.

I could upload it without their permission but I run the risk of either having adverts placed (which people hate), or getting banned entirely. Labels and artists will time after time refuse to grant licenses, because they'd rather let huge corporations like YouTube and CDBaby pocket most of the profit from monetizing videos with adverts just so they can make a trickle of income, than allow their work to be put in places that would boost viewership among people who might actually want to buy albums, merch, and live event tickets.
